Long-time dynamics of a nonlocal epidemic model with free boundaries: spreading-vanishing dichotomyThanks: ∗School of Science and Technology, University of New England, Armidale, NSW 2351, AustraliaThanks: Emails: ydu@une.edu.au (Y. Du), rwang3@myune.edu.au (R. Wang) Thanks: This research was supported by the Australian Research Coucile.

Rong Wang∗ and Yihong Du∗
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In this paper, we examine the long-time dynamics of an epidemic model whose diffusion and reaction terms involve nonlocal effects described by suitable convolution operators. The spreading front of the disease is represented by the free boundaries in the model. We show that the model is well-posed, its long-time dynamical behaviour is characterised by a spreading-vanishing dichotomy, and we also obtain sharp criteria to determine the dichotomy. Some of the nonlocal effects in the model pose extra difficulties in the mathematical treatment, which are dealt with by introducing new approaches. The model can capture accelerated spreading, and its spreading rate will be discussed in a subsequent work.

Key Words: nonlocal diffusion, free boundary, epidemic spreading

AMS Subject Classification (2010): 35R09, 35R35, 92D30

1. Introduction

In this paper, we examine the long-time dynamical behaviour of an epidemic model with nonlocal diffusion and free boundaries, which is a refined version of several previous epidemic models based on the following ODE system proposed by Capasso and Paveri-fontana [12], for the spread of oro-faecal transmitted disease such as cholera,

(1.1) u′=−a11​u+a12​v,v′=−a22​v+G⁡(u),t>0.u^{\prime}=-a_{11}u+a_{12}v,\ v^{\prime}=-a_{22}v+G(u),\ t>0.

In (1.1), uu denotes the average density of the infective agents (bacteria, virus, etc.), while vv represents the average density of the infective human population, both are functions of time tt. The constant a11a_{11} denotes the natural death rate of the agents, a12a_{12} represents the growth rate of the agents contributed by the infective humans, and a22a_{22} denotes the fatality rate of the infective human population. These rates are all positive. The function G⁡(u)G(u) represents the infective rate of humans, which is assumed to satisfy

  1. (G​1)(G1)

    : G∈C1​([0,∞)),G⁡(0)=0,G′​(z)>0​ for ​z≥0;G\in C^{1}([0,\infty)),\ G(0)=0,\ G^{\prime}(z)>0\ \mbox{ for }z\geq 0;

  2. (G​2)(G2)

    : G⁡(z)z\frac{G(z)}{z} is strictly decreasing and limz→+∞G⁡(z)z<a11​a22a12\lim_{z\rightarrow+\infty}\frac{G(z)}{z}<\frac{a_{11}a_{22}}{a_{12}}.

The dynamics of (1.1) is governed by the following threshold parameter, known as the basic reproduction number,

(1.2) R0:=a12​G′​(0)a11​a22.R_{0}:=\frac{a_{12}G^{\prime}(0)}{a_{11}a_{22}}.

Specifically, if R0<1R_{0}<1, the unique solution (u,v)(u,v) with initial values u⁡(0),v⁡(0)>0u(0),v(0)>0 goes to (0,0)(0,0) as t→∞t\to\infty; while if R0>1R_{0}>1, then (1.1) admits a unique positive equilibrium (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) and (u,v)→(u∗,v∗)(u,v)\to(u^{*},v^{*}) as t→∞t\to\infty. Clearly the pair (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) is uniquely determined by (when R0>1R_{0}>1)

(1.3) G⁡(u∗)u∗=a11​a22a12,v∗=a11a12​u∗.\frac{G(u^{*})}{u^{*}}=\frac{a_{11}a_{22}}{a_{12}},\;v^{*}=\frac{a_{11}}{a_{12}}u^{*}.

Over the years, this basic model has been refined many times along different directions. To include the effect of spatial movements of both the infectious agent and the infective human population in the epidemic, Capasso and Maddalena [13] considered the corresponding reaction-diffusion system to (1.1) over a bounded spatial domain with suitable boundary conditions, and they obtained similar (but slightly weaker) results on the long-term dynamics of the reaction-diffusion model, by replacing R0R_{0} with a number or numbers determined by certain eigenvalue problems. Their result was sharp when diffusion only appears in the equation for the infectious agents uu, assuming the mobility of the infective humans vv is relatively small and hence ignored in the model.

Many subsequent works also ignored the mobility of the infective humans. For example, in [30] and [35], in order to describe the spatial spreading of the disease, traveling wave solutions were obtained for the corresponding system

(1.4) {ut=d1​Δ​u−a11​u+a12​vin​ℝ×(0,+∞),vt=−a22​v+G⁡(u)in​ℝ×(0,+∞).\begin{cases}u_{t}=d_{1}\Delta u-a_{11}u+a_{12}v&~~\text{in}~~\mathbb{R}\times(0,+\infty),\\ v_{t}=-a_{22}v+G(u)&~~\text{in}~~\mathbb{R}\times(0,+\infty).\end{cases}

To capture the evolution of the spreading front of the disease, Ahn et al [1] investigated a free boundary version of (1.4), which is a special case of the following system (namely, with d2=ρ=0d_{2}=\rho=0),

(1.5) {ut=d1​ux​x−a11​u+a12​v,g⁡(t)<x⁡<h⁡(t),t>​0,vt=d2​vx​x−a22​v+G⁡(u),g⁡(t)<x⁡<h⁡(t),t>​0,u=v=0,x=h(t)orx=g(t),t>0,h′​(t)=−μ⁡[ux​(h⁡(t),t)+ρ​vx​(h⁡(t),t)],t>0,g′​(t)=−μ⁡[ux​(g⁡(t),t)+ρ​vx​(g⁡(t),t)],t>0,h(0)=h0,g(0)=−h0,u(x,0)=u0(x),v(x,0)=v0(x),−h0≤x≤h0,\begin{cases}u_{t}=d_{1}u_{xx}-a_{11}u+a_{12}v,&g(t)<x<h(t),~~t>0,\\ v_{t}=d_{2}v_{xx}-a_{22}v+G(u),&g(t)<x<h(t),~~t>0,\\ u=v=0,&x=h(t)~\mbox{or}~x=g(t),~t>0,\\ h^{\prime}(t)=-\mu[u_{x}(h(t),t)+\rho v_{x}(h(t),t)],&t>0,\\ g^{\prime}(t)=-\mu[u_{x}(g(t),t)+\rho v_{x}(g(t),t)],&t>0,\\ h(0)=h_{0},~g(0)=-h_{0},&\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),~~v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),&-h_{0}\leq x\leq h_{0},\end{cases}

where the epidemic region is represented by the evolving interval [g⁡(t),h⁡(t)][g(t),h(t)], with x=g⁡(t)x=g(t) and x=h⁡(t)x=h(t) giving the spreading fronts of the disease.

The general case of (1.5) with d2>0d_{2}>0 and ρ≥0\rho\geq 0 was considered by Wang and Du [29], where a rather complete description of the long-time dynamical behaviour of (1.5) was obtained, which in particular reveals the influence of d2d_{2} in the model. More precisely, with R0R_{0} given by (1.2), the epidemic modelled by (1.5) vanishes if R0≤1R_{0}\leq 1, i.e., as t→∞t\to\infty, the epidemic region [g⁡(t),h⁡(t)][g(t),h(t)] converges to a finite interval and (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))(u(x,t),v(x,t)) goes to (0,0)(0,0) uniformly in xx. If R0>1R_{0}>1, a spreading-vanishing dichotomy holds, namely either the epidemic vanishes as above, or it spreads successfully in the sense that [g⁡(t),h⁡(t)][g(t),h(t)] converges to (−∞,∞)(-\infty,\infty) and (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))→(u∗,v∗)(u(x,t),v(x,t))\to(u^{*},v^{*}) locally uniformly in xx as t→∞t\to\infty. Furthermore, a critical length L∗L^{*} independent of the initial data (u0,v0,h0)(u_{0},v_{0},h_{0}) was found such that, if the range radius of the initial infected region h0≥L∗h_{0}\geq L^{*}, then the spreading is always successful, while if h0<L∗h_{0}<L^{*}, then there exists μ∗>0\mu^{*}>0 depending on (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) such that vanishing occurs when 0<μ≤μ∗0<\mu\leq\mu^{*} and spreading persists when μ>μ∗\mu>\mu^{*}. Moreover, when spreading persists, it has a finite asymptotic speed, i.e., −limt→∞g(t)/t=limt→∞h(t)/t=c0>0-\lim_{t\to\infty}g(t)/t=\lim_{t\to\infty}h(t)/t=c_{0}>0, with c0c_{0} determined by an associated semi-wave problem.

When d2=ρ=0d_{2}=\rho=0 in problem (1.5), the spreading-vanishing dichotomy was first obtained by Ahn et al. [1], and the spreading speed for this case was obtained by Zhao et al. [32].

The effect of d2d_{2} on the dynamics of (1.5) can be partly seen from the formula for the critical number L∗L^{*}, which is given by

L∗:=π2​d1​a22+d2​a11+(d1​a22+d2​a11)2+4​d1​d2​a11​a22​(R0−1)2​a11​a22​(R0−1).L^{*}:=\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\frac{d_{1}a_{22}+d_{2}a_{11}+\sqrt{(d_{1}a_{22}+d_{2}a_{11})^{2}+4d_{1}d_{2}a_{11}a_{22}(R_{0}-1)}}{2a_{11}a_{22}(R_{0}-1)}}.

So L∗L^{*} is increasing in d2d_{2}, implying that the chance of successful spreading of the epidemic is decreased when d2d_{2} is increased, which might appear counter intuitive on first sight, but it is in agreement with result already arising in the reaction-diffusion model over a bounded domain considered by Capasso and Maddalena [13] mentioned above.

In (1.5), the spatial movements of infectious agents and humans are assumed to follow the rule of Brownian motion, represented by the “local diffusion” terms d1​ux​xd_{1}u_{xx} and d2​vx​xd_{2}v_{xx}. However, in reality the movements of infectious agents and infective humans often contain nonlocal factors such as long-distance dispersal caused by modern ways of transportation, for example. To include such nonlocal dispersal factors, one widely used approach is to replace the local diffusion terms d1​ux​xd_{1}u_{xx} and d2​vx​xd_{2}v_{xx} by, respectively,

d1​∫ℝJ1​(x−y)​u​(y,t)​dy−d1​u​(x,t)​ and ​d2​∫ℝJ2​(x−y)​v​(y,t)​dy−d2​v​(x,t),\displaystyle d_{1}\int_{\mathbb{R}}J_{1}(x-y)u(y,t)dy-d_{1}u(x,t)\mbox{ and }d_{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}J_{2}(x-y)v(y,t)dy-d_{2}v(x,t),

where Ji​(x)J_{i}(x) (i=1,2)(i=1,2) is a continuous function satisfying

  1. (J)

    Ji∈C⁡(ℝ)∩L∞​(ℝ)J_{i}\in C(\mathbb{R})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), JiJ_{i} is symmetric and nonnegative, Ji​(0)>0J_{i}(0)>0, ∫ℝJi​(x)​𝑑x=1\int_{\mathbb{R}}J_{i}(x)dx=1.

Roughly speaking, the nonlocal diffusion term ∫ℝJ1​(x−y)​u​(y,t)​𝑑y−u⁡(x,t)\int_{\mathbb{R}}J_{1}(x-y)u(y,t)dy-u(x,t) is obtained from the assumption that an individual of uu at location yy and time tt has probability J1​(x−y)J_{1}(x-y) to move to location xx in a time unit.

When the local diffusion terms in (1.5) are replaced by the above nonlocal diffusion terms, as in Cao et al. [10], the free boundary conditions need to be modified accordingly, and the local diffusion model (1.5) becomes

Here, following Capasso [11], we have also replaced the term c12​v​(x,t)c_{12}v(x,t) in (1.5) by

(1.7) a12​∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)K⁡(x−y)​v​(y,t)​𝑑y\displaystyle a_{12}\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}K(x-y)v(y,t)dy

in (1.6), to represent the more realistic and consistant assumption that the contribution to the growth of the infectious agents at location xx by the infective humans is also nonlocal. Indeed, in most societies, the human wastes, which are the main sources of the infectious agents in this model, are moved away immediately from the exact location of the infective humans. Therefore the contribution to uu at location xx is usually from infective humans in a neighbourhood of xx, which is better represented by a nonlocal operator. If K⁡(x)K(x) is equal to the Dirac delta function δ0​(x)\delta_{0}(x), then

a12​∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)K⁡(x−y)​v​(y,t)​𝑑y=a12​v​(x,t)\displaystyle a_{12}\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}K(x-y)v(y,t)dy=a_{12}v(x,t) for x∈(g⁡(t),h⁡(t))x\in(g(t),h(t));

we will assume that KK satisfies (J) and so the term (1.7) represents a true nonlocal effect.

The initial functions u0​(x)u_{0}(x) and v0​(x)v_{0}(x) in (1.6) are assumed to satisfy

(1.8) {u0∈C[−h0,h0],u0(±h0)=0andu0(x)>0forx∈(−h0,h0),v0∈C[−h0,h0],v0(±h0)=0andv0(x)>0forx∈(−h0,h0).\left\{\begin{aligned} &u_{0}\in C[-h_{0},h_{0}],~~u_{0}(\pm h_{0})=0~~\text{and}~~u_{0}(x)>0~~\mbox{for}~~x\in(-h_{0},h_{0}),\\ &v_{0}\in C[-h_{0},h_{0}],~~v_{0}(\pm h_{0})=0~~\text{and}~~v_{0}(x)>0~~\mbox{for}~~x\in(-h_{0},h_{0}).\end{aligned}\right.

The main purpose of this paper is to obtain a good understanding of the long-time dynamics of (1.6). Several special cases or closely related cases of (1.6) have already been considered in the recent literature. When d2=ρ=0d_{2}=\rho=0 and K​(x)=δ0​(x)K(x)=\delta_{0}(x) so the term a12​∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)K⁡(x−y)​v​(y,t)​𝑑y\displaystyle a_{12}\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}K(x-y)v(y,t)dy is changed back to a12​v​(x,t)a_{12}v(x,t), problem (1.6) becomes a precise nonlocal diffusion version of (1.5) with d2=0d_{2}=0; for this special case, Zhao et al. [34] proved that the problem is well posed mathematically and the long-time dynamics of the model is governed by a spreading-vanishing dichotomy, similar to its local diffusion version, but differences arise in the criteria distinguishing the alternatives in the dichotomy. More striking differences appear when results of Du and Ni in [20] on the rate of spreading were applied to this case of the model. It follows from [20] that when J1J_{1} satisfies an additional threshold condition, then when spreading persisits, −limt→∞g(t)/t=limt→∞h(t)/t-\lim_{t\to\infty}g(t)/t=\lim_{t\to\infty}h(t)/t exists and is a finite number determined by an associated semi-wave problem, while −limt→∞g(t)/t=limt→∞h(t)/t=∞-\lim_{t\to\infty}g(t)/t=\lim_{t\to\infty}h(t)/t=\infty when this threshold condition is not satisfied by J1J_{1} (note that since d2=ρ=0d_{2}=\rho=0, J2J_{2} does not appear in this case of the model). This latter case is known as “accelerated spreading”, and was first shown to occur for a nonlocal free boundary problem for the Fisher-KPP model in [18].

These results were extended by Zhao et al. [33] and Du et al. [17] to the case of (1.6) with d2=ρ=0d_{2}=\rho=0, and by Chang and Du [14] for (1.6) with d2>0,ρ≥0d_{2}>0,\rho\geq 0 and the term a12​∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)K⁡(x−y)​v​(y,t)​𝑑y\displaystyle a_{12}\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}K(x-y)v(y,t)dy replaced by a12​v​(x,t)a_{12}v(x,t). Moreover, the rate of accelerated spreading was given in [14] when Ji​(x)∼|x|−γJ_{i}(x)\sim|x|^{-\gamma} for |x|≫1|x|\gg 1 with γ∈(1,2]\gamma\in(1,2] (see Theorem 1.6 there for details, which follow from more general results due to Du and Ni).

A West Nile virus model with nonlocal diffusion and free boundaries was studied by Du and Ni [19], which share some similarities to (1.6) in that it is also a cooperative evolution system, and its spreading speed can be treated by the same genera approach in [20]. The nonlocal term a12​∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)K⁡(x−y)​v​(y,t)​𝑑y\displaystyle a_{12}\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}K(x-y)v(y,t)dy in (1.6) renders it outside the scope of [20], and moreover, it causes several technical difficulties which require very different treatment from the earlier works.

There is a large literature on related nonlocal diffusion problems over the entire spatial space ℝ\mathbb{R} or ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}, without involving any free boundaries; a small sample of these works can be found in [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 15, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 31] and the references therein.

Let us now describe the main results for (1.6) precisely.

Theorem 1.1 (Global existence and uniqueness).

Suppose that J1​(x),J2​(x)J_{1}(x),J_{2}(x) and K⁡(x)K(x) satisfy assumption (J), GG satisfies (G​1)(G1)-(G​2)(G2), and (u0​(x),v0​(x))(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x)) satisfies (1.8). Then problem (1.6) admits a unique solution defined for all t>0t>0.

Theorem 1.2 (Spreading-vanishing dichotomy).

Under the conditions of Theorem 1.1, suppose that (u,v,g,h)(u,v,g,h) is the solution of (1.6); then

h∞:=limt→∞h(t)∈(h0,∞]andg∞:=limt→∞g(t)∈[−∞,−h0) exist,h_{\infty}:=\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}h(t)\in(h_{0},\infty]~\mbox{and}~g_{\infty}:=\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}g(t)\in[-\infty,-h_{0})\mbox{ exist},

and one of the following cases must occur:

  • (i)

    Vanishing:

    h∞−g∞<∞​and​limt→∞(u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))=(0,0)​uniformly for​x∈[g⁡(t),h⁡(t)];h_{\infty}-g_{\infty}<\infty~~\text{and}~~\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(u(x,t),v(x,t))=(0,0)~~\mbox{uniformly for}~~x\in[g(t),h(t)];
  • (ii)

    Spreading:

    h∞=−g∞=∞​and​limt→∞(u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))=(u∗,v∗)​locally uniformly in​ℝ.h_{\infty}=-g_{\infty}=\infty~~\text{and}~~\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(u(x,t),v(x,t))=(u^{*},v^{*})~~\mbox{locally uniformly in}~~\mathbb{R}.
Theorem 1.3 (Spreading-vanishing criteria).

Let R0R_{0} be given by (1.2). Then the alternatives in Theorem 1.2 are determined as follows:

  • (i)

    If R0≤1R_{0}\leq 1, then vanishing always occurs.

  • (ii)

    If R0>1R_{0}>1, then there exists a critical length l∗>0l^{*}>0 independent of the initial data (u0,v0,h0)(u_{0},v_{0},h_{0}) such that if h0≥l∗h_{0}\geq l^{*}, then spreading always persists, while if h0<l∗h_{0}<l^{*}, then there exists μ∗>0\mu^{*}>0 depending on (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) such that vanishing happens when μ∈(0,μ∗]\mu\in(0,\mu^{*}] and spreading persists when μ∈(μ∗,∞)\mu\in(\mu^{*},\infty).

When spreading persists, the spreading speed will be determined in a subsequent work. In particular we will find threshold conditions on J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} which determine whether the speed is finite or infinite.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, we give some comparison principles to be used throughout the paper; the proofs of some of them depend on the existence uniqueness theorem (Theorem 1.1), whose proof is postponed to the last section of the paper, Section 5, since it is only a relatively simple modification of existing proofs in the literature. Section 3 treats the corresponding fixed boundary problem and the associated eigenvalue problem. Here the nonlocal term ∫−llK⁡(x−y)​v​(y,t)​𝑑y\int_{-l}^{l}K(x-y)v(y,t)dy induces nontrivial technical difficulties, especially for the eigenvalue problem. A new approach is used in this section to obtain the desired results, which we believe should have applications elsewhere. In Section 4, we make use of the results in Section 3 to prove the spreading-vanishing dichotomy and obtain the sharp criteria governing this dichotomy. As already mentioned, Section 5 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.1.

2. Some basic results

In this section, we collect some comparison results, which form the basis of this research. For convenience of later discussions, we introduce some notations first. For any given 𝐮=(u1,v1),𝐯=(v1,v2)∈ℝ2\mathbf{u}=(u_{1},v_{1}),\mathbf{v}=(v_{1},v_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, we denote

In this section, we consider the associated fixed boundary problem of (1.6), namely the system with

(3.1) {ut=d1​∫−llJ1​(x−y)​u​(y,t)​𝑑y−d1​u−a11​u+a12∫−llK(x−y)v(y,t)dy,t>0,x∈(−l,l),vt=d2​∫−llJ2​(x−y)​v​(y,t)​dy−d2​v−a22​v+G⁡(u),t>0,x∈(−l,l),u(x,0)=u0(x),v(x,0)=v0(x),x∈[−l,−l],\begin{cases}\displaystyle u_{t}=d_{1}\int_{-l}^{l}J_{1}(x-y)u(y,t)dy-d_{1}u-a_{11}u&\\ \displaystyle\hskip 76.82234pt+a_{12}\int_{-l}^{l}K(x-y)v(y,t)dy,&t>0,~~x\in(-l,l),\\ \displaystyle v_{t}=d_{2}\int_{-l}^{l}J_{2}(x-y)v(y,t)dy-d_{2}v-a_{22}v+G(u),&t>0,~~x\in(-l,l),\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),~~~v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),&x\in[-l,-l],\end{cases}

where

(0,0)⪯(u0,v0)∈C​([−l,l])2.(0,0)\preceq(u_{0},v_{0})\in C([-l,l])^{2}.

It turns out that here rather different techniques are needed from previous works where the nonlocal term a12​∫−llK⁡(x−y)​u​(y,t)​𝑑ya_{12}\int_{-l}^{l}K(x-y)u(y,t)dy in (3.1) was replaced by a12​u​(x,t)a_{12}u(x,t). Note that a good understanding of the behaviour of this fixed boundary problem is crucial for determining the long-time behaviour of (1.6).

3.1. The associated eigenvalue problem

The long-time dynamical behaviour of (3.1) is governed by its linearised eigenvalue problem at the trivial solution (0,0)(0,0), which has the form

(3.2) {d1​∫−llJ1​(x−y)​θ1​(y)​dy−d1​θ1−a11​θ1+a12​∫−llK⁡(x−y)​θ2​(y)​dy=λ​θ1,x∈[−l,l],d2​∫−llJ2​(x−y)​θ2​(y)​dy−d2​θ2−a22​θ2+G′​(0)​θ1=λ​θ2,x∈[−l,l].\begin{cases}\displaystyle d_{1}\int_{-l}^{l}J_{1}(x-y)\theta_{1}(y)dy-d_{1}\theta_{1}-a_{11}\theta_{1}\displaystyle+a_{12}\int_{-l}^{l}K(x-y)\theta_{2}(y)dy=\lambda\theta_{1},&x\in[-l,l],\\ \displaystyle d_{2}\int_{-l}^{l}J_{2}(x-y)\theta_{2}(y)dy-d_{2}\theta_{2}-a_{22}\theta_{2}+G^{\prime}(0)\theta_{1}=\lambda\theta_{2},&x\in[-l,l].\\ \end{cases}

{D+:={𝜽∈D∣θ1(x),θ2(x)≥0,x∈[−l,l]},D+0:={𝜽∈D∣θ1(x),θ2(x)>0,x∈[−l,l]}.\begin{cases}D_{+}:=\{\bm{\theta}\in D\mid\theta_{1}(x),\theta_{2}(x)\geq 0,x\in[-l,l]\},\\ D_{+}^{0}:=\{\bm{\theta}\in D\mid\theta_{1}(x),\theta_{2}(x)>0,x\in[-l,l]\}.\end{cases}

for 𝜽=(θ1,θ2)∈D\bm{\theta}=(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})\in D. Then (3.2) can be rewritten as

Throughout this section, we always assume that J1,J2J_{1},J_{2} and KK satisfy (J), and GG satisfies (G1) and (G2).

Lemma 3.1.

The eigenvalue problem

(3.3) {(d1+a11)​θ1​(x)−a12​∫−llK⁡(x−y)​θ2​(y)​dy=λ​θ1​(x),x∈[−l,l],−G′​(0)​θ1​(x)+(d2+a22)​θ2​(x)=λ​θ2​(x),x∈[−l,l]\begin{cases}\displaystyle(d_{1}+a_{11})\theta_{1}(x)-a_{12}\int_{-l}^{l}K(x-y)\theta_{2}(y)dy=\lambda\theta_{1}(x),&x\in[-l,l],\\ \displaystyle-G^{\prime}(0)\theta_{1}(x)+(d_{2}+a_{22})\theta_{2}(x)=\lambda\theta_{2}(x),&x\in[-l,l]\\ \end{cases}

admits a unique real eigenvalue denoted by λ1\lambda_{1} whose corresponding eigenfunction pair (θ1,θ2)∈D+0({\theta}_{1},{\theta}_{2})\in D_{+}^{0}.

Proof.

We first consider the following eigenvalue problem:

(3.4) ∫−llK⁡(x−y)​θ2​(y)​𝑑y=λ~​θ2​(x)​ for ​x∈[−l,l].\int_{-l}^{l}K(x-y)\theta_{2}(y)dy=\tilde{\lambda}\,\theta_{2}(x)\mbox{ for }x\in[-l,l].

It follows from Theorem 3.1 in [24] that (3.4) admits a positive principal eigenvalue λ~\tilde{\lambda} given by

(3.5) λ~=supθ∗∈L2​([−l,l]),‖θ∗‖≠0∫−ll∫−llK⁡(x−y)​θ∗​(x)​θ∗​(y)​𝑑y​𝑑x∫−llθ∗2​(x)​𝑑x\tilde{\lambda}=\sup_{\theta_{*}\in L^{2}([-l,l]),\|\theta_{*}\|\neq 0}\frac{\displaystyle\int_{-l}^{l}\int_{-l}^{l}K(x-y)\theta_{*}(x)\theta_{*}(y)dydx}{\displaystyle\int_{-l}^{l}\theta_{*}^{2}(x)dx}\\

and a unique (up to a scalar multiple) corresponding positive eigenfunction θ∗​(x)\theta_{*}(x). Note that problem (3.3) can be rewritten as

∫−llK⁡(x−y)​θ2​(y)​𝑑y=(d1+a11−λ)​(d2+a22−λ)a12​G′​(0)​θ2​(y).\int_{-l}^{l}K(x-y)\theta_{2}(y)dy=\frac{(d_{1}+a_{11}-\lambda)(d_{2}+a_{22}-\lambda)}{a_{12}G^{\prime}(0)}\theta_{2}(y).

Let

(3.6) (d1+a11−λ)​(d2+a22−λ)a12​G′​(0)=λ~.\frac{(d_{1}+a_{11}-\lambda)(d_{2}+a_{22}-\lambda)}{a_{12}G^{\prime}(0)}=\tilde{\lambda}.

Simple calculations show that the above identity holds when λ\lambda takes the following values λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2}:

λ1=(d1+a11+d2+a22)−(d1+a11−d2−a22)2+4​a12​G′​(0)​λ~2,\displaystyle\lambda_{1}=\frac{(d_{1}+a_{11}+d_{2}+a_{22})-\sqrt{(d_{1}+a_{11}-d_{2}-a_{22})^{2}+4a_{12}G^{\prime}(0)\tilde{\lambda}}}{2},
λ2=(d1+a11+d2+a22)+(d1+a11−d2−a22)2+4​a12​G′​(0)​λ~2.\displaystyle\lambda_{2}=\frac{(d_{1}+a_{11}+d_{2}+a_{22})+\sqrt{(d_{1}+a_{11}-d_{2}-a_{22})^{2}+4a_{12}G^{\prime}(0)\tilde{\lambda}}}{2}.

When we take θ~:=(θ~1,θ~2)=(δ1​θ∗,θ∗)\tilde{\theta}:=(\tilde{\theta}_{1},\tilde{\theta}_{2})=(\delta_{1}\theta_{*},\theta_{*}) with

δ1:=d2+a22−λ1G′​(0)>0,\delta_{1}:=\frac{d_{2}+a_{22}-\lambda_{1}}{G^{\prime}(0)}>0,

it is easily checked that (δ1​θ∗,θ∗)(\delta_{1}\theta_{*},\theta_{*}) is a positive solution of (3.3) with λ=λ1\lambda=\lambda_{1}. When λ=λ2\lambda=\lambda_{2}, (θ~1,θ~2)=(δ2​θ∗,θ∗)(\tilde{\theta}_{1},\tilde{\theta}_{2})=(\delta_{2}\theta_{*},\theta_{*}) solve (3.3) with

δ2:=d2+a22−λ2G′​(0)<0.\delta_{2}:=\frac{d_{2}+a_{22}-\lambda_{2}}{G^{\prime}(0)}<0.

Conversely, if (θ1,θ2)∈D+0(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})\in D_{+}^{0} is a solution of (3.3), then necessarily θ2\theta_{2} is a positive solution of (3.4) with λ~\tilde{\lambda} defined in (3.6) and thus

θ1=d2+a22−λG′​(0)​θ2.\theta_{1}=\frac{d_{2}+a_{22}-\lambda}{G^{\prime}(0)}\theta_{2}.

It follows from the positivity of (θ1,θ2)(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}) that λ<d2+a22\lambda<d_{2}+a_{22} and hence λ=λ1\lambda=\lambda_{1}. ∎

Lemma 3.2.

The following statements are valid:

  • (i​i​i)(iii)

with

Lemma 3.3.

For each α>−λ1\alpha>-\lambda_{1}, 𝒥​(𝒯+α​𝐈)−1\mathcal{J}(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1} and (𝒯+α​𝐈)−1​𝒥(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathcal{J} are both compact and strongly positive operators.

Proof.

It follows from Lemma 3.2 that (𝒯+α​𝐈)−1(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1} is a bounded strongly positive linear operator for any α>−λ1\alpha>-\lambda_{1}. We now prove that 𝒥\mathcal{J} is compact. Let {𝐮𝐧}⊂D\{\mathbf{{u_{n}}}\}\subset D be a bounded sequence. Define 𝐯𝐧=𝒥​𝐮𝐧\mathbf{v_{n}}=\mathcal{J}\mathbf{u_{n}}. It follows from assumption (J) that {𝐯𝐧}\{\mathbf{v_{n}}\} is bounded and equicontinuous. By the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem, {𝐯𝐧}\{\mathbf{v_{n}}\} is precompact. Hence, 𝒥\mathcal{J} is a compact operator.

Moreover, it is also easily seen that if (θ1,θ2)∈D+∖{𝟎}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})\in D_{+}\setminus\{\bf 0\}, then 𝒥⁡(θ1,θ2)∈D+∖{𝟎}\mathcal{J}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})\in D_{+}\setminus\{\bf 0\}, and if (θ1,θ2)∈D+0(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})\in D_{+}^{0}, then 𝒥⁡(θ1,θ2)∈D+0\mathcal{J}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})\in D_{+}^{0}. Thus 𝒥​(𝒯+α​𝐈)−1\mathcal{J}(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1} and (𝒯+α​𝐈)−1​𝒥(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathcal{J} are both compact and strongly positive for any α>−λ1\alpha>-\lambda_{1}. This finishes the proof. ∎

Lemma 3.4.

For α>−λ1\alpha>-\lambda_{1}, denote by r⁡(α):=r⁡(𝒥​(𝒯+α​𝐈)−1)r(\alpha):=r(\mathcal{J}(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1}) the spectral radius of 𝒥​(𝒯+α​𝐈)−1\mathcal{J}(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1}. Then the following statements are valid:

  • (i)(i)

    r⁡((𝒯+α​𝐈)−1​𝒥)=r⁡(α)r((\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathcal{J})=r(\alpha),

  • (i​i)(ii)

    limα↘−λ1r⁡(α)=∞\lim_{\alpha\searrow-\lambda_{1}}r(\alpha)=\infty,

  • (i​i​i)(iii)

    limα→∞r⁡(α)=0\lim_{\alpha\rightarrow\infty}r(\alpha)=0,

  • (i​v)(iv)

    r⁡(α)r(\alpha) is continuous and strictly decreasing for α>−λ1\alpha>-\lambda_{1}.

(i)(i) By Lemma 3.3 and the Krein-Rutman Theorem, r⁡(α)=r⁡(𝒥​(𝒯+α​I)−1)r(\alpha)=r(\mathcal{J}(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\textbf{I})^{-1}) is the unique eigenvalue which corresponds to an eigenvector Φ∈D+0\Phi\in D_{+}^{0}, namely

Letting Ψ:=(𝒯+α​I)−1​Φ\Psi:=(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\textbf{I})^{-1}\Phi, then

(𝒯+α​I)−1​𝒥​Ψ=r⁡(α)​Ψ,Ψ∈D+0.(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\textbf{I})^{-1}\mathcal{J}\Psi=r(\alpha)\Psi,\;\Psi\in D_{+}^{0}.

Applying the Krein-Rutman theorem to (𝒯+α​I)−1​𝒥(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\textbf{I})^{-1}\mathcal{J}, we similarly conclude that r⁡((𝒯+α​𝐈)−1​𝒥)r((\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathcal{J}) is the only eigenvalue which corresponds to an eigenvector in D+0D_{+}^{0}. Thus the above identity implies that r⁡(α)=r⁡((𝒯+α​𝐈)−1​𝒥)r(\alpha)=r((\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathcal{J}). This proves (i)(i).

(i​i)(ii) By Lemma 3.1 and Lemma 3.2, for x∈[−l,l]x\in[-l,l], we have, with 𝜽~=(θ~1,θ~2)=(δ1​θ∗,θ∗)\bm{\tilde{\theta}}=(\tilde{\theta}_{1},\tilde{\theta}_{2})=(\delta_{1}\theta_{*},\theta_{*}),

𝒥​(𝒯+α​𝑰)−1​(θ~1,θ~2)​(x)=(d1λ1+α​∫−llJ1​(x−y)​θ~1​(y)​𝑑yd2λ1+α​∫−llJ2​(x−y)​θ~2​(y)​𝑑y)T.\mathcal{J}(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\bm{I})^{-1}(\tilde{\theta}_{1},\tilde{\theta}_{2})(x)=\left(\begin{matrix}\displaystyle\frac{d_{1}}{\lambda_{1}+\alpha}\int^{l}_{-l}J_{1}(x-y)\tilde{\theta}_{1}(y)dy\\ \displaystyle\frac{d_{2}}{\lambda_{1}+\alpha}\int^{l}_{-l}J_{2}(x-y)\tilde{\theta}_{2}(y)dy\\ \end{matrix}\right)^{T}.

It follows from (J) that there exist a small constant ε>0\varepsilon>0 and some positive constant δ0>0\delta^{0}>0 such that, for i=1,2i=1,2,

Ji​(x−y)≥δ0​ if ​|x−y|≤ε.J_{i}(x-y)\geq\delta^{0}\mbox{ if }|x-y|\leq\varepsilon.

Let θ~m:=minx∈[−l,l]⁡min⁡{θ~1​(x),θ~2​(x)}\tilde{\theta}_{m}:=\min_{x\in[-l,l]}\min\{\tilde{\theta}_{1}(x),\tilde{\theta}_{2}(x)\}. Then

∫−llJi​(x−y)​θ~i​(y)​𝑑y≥ε​δ0​θ~m​ for any ​x∈[−l,l].\displaystyle\int^{l}_{-l}J_{i}(x-y)\tilde{\theta}_{i}(y)dy\geq\varepsilon\delta^{0}\tilde{\theta}_{m}\mbox{ for any }x\in[-l,l].

Since

limα↘−λ11λ1+α=∞,\displaystyle\lim_{\alpha\searrow-\lambda_{1}}\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}+\alpha}=\infty,

given any γ>1\gamma>1, for 0<α+λ1≪10<\alpha+\lambda_{1}\ll 1 we thus have

‖(𝒥​(𝒯+α​𝐈)−1)n‖​‖𝜽~‖≥‖(𝒥​(𝒯+α​𝐈)−1)n​𝜽~‖≥γn​‖𝜽~‖.\|(\mathcal{J}(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1})^{n}\|\|\bm{\tilde{\theta}}\|\geq\|(\mathcal{J}(\mathcal{T}+\alpha\mathbf{I})^{-1})^{n}\bm{\tilde{\theta}}\|\geq\gamma^{n}\|\bm{\tilde{\theta}}\|.

Lemma 4.5.

h∞<∞h_{\infty}<\infty if only and only if −g∞<∞-g_{\infty}<\infty.

Proof.

By way of contradiction, we assume that h∞<∞h_{\infty}<\infty and −g∞=∞-g_{\infty}=\infty. Then we see that h∞−g∞=∞h_{\infty}-g_{\infty}=\infty and thus by Lemma 4.2, R0>1R_{0}>1 must hold. Due to g∞=∞g_{\infty}=\infty, there exists a large TT such that for all t≥Tt\geq T, h⁡(t)−g⁡(t)>2​l∗h(t)-g(t)>2l^{*}. It follows from (i​i)(ii) of Proposition 3.9 that λ0​(g⁡(t),h⁡(t))>0\lambda_{0}(g(t),h(t))>0 for such t≥Tt\geq T. Since h∞−g∞=∞h_{\infty}-g_{\infty}=\infty, similar to (4.3), we can find some constant c2>0c_{2}>0 such that for some large T0>TT^{0}>T,

h′​(t)=μ​∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)∫h⁡(t)∞J1​(x−y)​u​(x,t)​𝑑y​d+μ​ρ​∫g⁡(t)h⁡(t)∫h⁡(t)∞J2​(x−y)​v​(x,t)​𝑑y​𝑑x>c2​ for ​t>T0,\displaystyle h^{\prime}(t)=\mu\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}\int^{\infty}_{h(t)}J_{1}(x-y)u(x,t)dyd+\mu\rho\int_{g(t)}^{h(t)}\int^{\infty}_{h(t)}J_{2}(x-y)v(x,t)dydx>c_{2}\mbox{ for }t>T^{0},

which contradicts h⁡(t)<∞h(t)<\infty for all t>0t>0. Therefore, if h∞<∞h_{\infty}<\infty holds, we have −g∞<∞-g_{\infty}<\infty. Similarly we can show that −g∞<∞-g_{\infty}<\infty and h∞=∞h_{\infty}=\infty lead to a contradiction. ∎

Lemma 4.6.

If R0>1R_{0}>1 and h0≥l∗h_{0}\geq l^{*}, then h∞=−g∞=∞h_{\infty}=-g_{\infty}=\infty and

limt→∞(u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))=(u∗,v∗)​ locally uniformly in ​ℝ,\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(u(x,t),v(x,t))=(u^{*},v^{*})\mbox{ locally uniformly in }\mathbb{R},

where (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) is defined in (1.3).

Proof.

If R0>1R_{0}>1 and h0≥l∗h_{0}\geq l^{*}, by (i​i)(ii) of Proposition 3.9, for any t>0t>0, we have λ0​(g⁡(t),h⁡(t))>0\lambda_{0}(g(t),h(t))>0, where λ0​(g⁡(t),h⁡(t))\lambda_{0}(g(t),h(t)) is the unique eigenvalue of (3.2) with [−l,l][-l,l] replaced by [g⁡(t),h⁡(t)][g(t),h(t)]. Since (g⁡(t),h⁡(t))⊂(g∞,h∞)(g(t),h(t))\subset(g_{\infty},h_{\infty}) for t>0t>0, λ0​(g∞,h∞)>0\lambda_{0}(g_{\infty},h_{\infty})>0 holds. By Lemma 4.1, we have h∞−g∞=∞h_{\infty}-g_{\infty}=\infty. Lemma 4.5 shows that h∞=−g∞=∞h_{\infty}=-g_{\infty}=\infty.

Next we will prove the second assertion by showing the limit superior and limit inferior of the solution of (1.6) are both (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}). We first consider the limit inferior of this solution. Due to λ0​(g⁡(T),h⁡(T))>0\lambda_{0}(g(T),h(T))>0 for any fixed T>0T>0, we define by (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) the unique positive solution of (3.1) in [g⁡(T),h⁡(T)]×(0,∞)[g(T),h(T)]\times(0,\infty) with initial function pair (u~​(x,0),v~​(x,0))=(u⁡(x,T),v⁡(x,T)CLOSE(\tilde{u}(x,0),\tilde{v}(x,0))=(u(x,T),v(x,T). By applying Proposition 3.10, we see

limt→∞(u~​(x,t),v~​(x,t))=(w⁡(x),z⁡(x))​ uniformly for ​x∈[g⁡(T),h⁡(T)],\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(\tilde{u}(x,t),\tilde{v}(x,t))=(w(x),z(x))\mbox{ uniformly for }x\in[g(T),h(T)],

where (w⁡(x),z⁡(x))(w(x),z(x)) is the unique solution of problem (3.23) with [−l,l][-l,l] replaced by [g⁡(T),h⁡(T)][g(T),h(T)]. Similar to (4.2) we see that for any t>0t>0,

(u~​(x,t),v~​(x,t))⪯(u⁡(x,t+T),v⁡(x,t+T))​ for ​x∈[g⁡(T),h⁡(T)],\displaystyle(\tilde{u}(x,t),\tilde{v}(x,t))\preceq(u(x,t+T),v(x,t+T))\mbox{ for }x\in[g(T),h(T)],

which implies that

(w⁡(x),z⁡(x))⪯lim inft→∞(u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))​ for ​x∈[g⁡(T),h⁡(T)].\displaystyle(w(x),z(x))\preceq\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}(u(x,t),v(x,t))\mbox{ for }x\in[g(T),h(T)].

Since (g⁡(T),h⁡(T))→(−∞,∞)(g(T),h(T))\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty) as T→∞T\rightarrow\infty, by Lemma 3.11, we see that

(u∗,v∗)⪯lim inft→∞(u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))​ locally uniformly in ​ℝ.\displaystyle(u^{*},v^{*})\preceq\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}(u(x,t),v(x,t))\mbox{ locally uniformly in }\mathbb{R}.

Finally we will consider the limit superior of the solution of (1.6). Denote by (u¯​(t),v¯​(t))(\bar{u}(t),\bar{v}(t)) the unique solution of (1.1) with initial function pair (M1,M2)=(‖u0‖∞,‖v0‖∞)(M_{1},M_{2})=(\|u_{0}\|_{\infty},\|v_{0}\|_{\infty}). It is easily checked that (u¯,v¯)(\bar{u},\bar{v}) is an upper solution of problem (1.6), and hence

(u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))⪯(u¯​(t),v¯​(t))​ for ​t>0,x∈[g⁡(t),h⁡(t)].\displaystyle(u(x,t),v(x,t))\preceq(\bar{u}(t),\bar{v}(t))\mbox{ for }t>0,~x\in[g(t),h(t)].

Since R0>1R_{0}>1, we have

limt→∞(u¯​(t),v¯​(t))=(u∗,v∗),\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(\bar{u}(t),\bar{v}(t))=(u^{*},v^{*}),

which implies that the limit superior of (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))(u(x,t),v(x,t)) is (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) uniformly in xx. This finishes the proof. ∎

Lemma 4.7.

Step 4: Global existence and uniqueness.

This step can be proved by the same argument used in the proof of Theorem 2.1 in [21], and we omit the details. ∎
